<reason>Both sides were sharp and adapted round to round, but PRO built the cleaner path. PRO's core mechanism — project panels score forward-looking prophecies on preliminary data and therefore systematically favor the safe bet — was never directly denied by CON, who instead defended competition on procedural grounds (rotation, appeal, pluralism, visibility). PRO answered both pressure questions squarely: the person-vs-idea distinction (retrospective evidence vs forward bets) was a genuine answer to CON's best question, and the national allocation answer (base funding plus results-based redistribution, citing the British and Max Planck models) addressed the "elite-only" scaling critique, which CON's closing simply repeated without engaging. CON's strongest live route — a single early gatekeeper with no "next door" — was real and well pressed, but its chosen exhibit backfired: PRO showed Karikó was rejected by public competition for a decade and rescued by industry, which exists under either system; CON's reply that industry is something "only a project-based ecosystem creates" was asserted, not argued. PRO's crystallization ("a hierarchy adjusted by results or by promises"; "what does the extra gate buy?") made the decision easier than CON's "second chance" frame. PRO's clipped rebuttal is a minor execution cost that did not lose substance.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The Karikó exchange: CON deployed her as proof that outsiders need competitive doors; PRO reversed it in R1, pressed it in Q1, and sealed it in R2/closing — public competition said no for ten years and the rescuer was industry, so CON's best exhibit for competition is a case competition failed. CON's counter (pluralism, "keep knocking") never recovered the example.</best_rebuttal>
